questions.q: What separates a finite game from an infinite one?
a: A finite game has fixed players and rules and ends with a winner
A finite game has no audience, while an infinite game has one
A finite game changes its rules, while an infinite game keeps them
A finite game is played for fun, while an infinite game is played for money
questions.why: Lesson 1 says finite games end in a winner, while infinite games aim to keep going.

questions.q: Why is a career closer to an infinite game than a job is?
a: It has no fixed rules or final winner, and the work can outlast you
It always involves competing directly against other people
It ends at a clear moment when a title has been earned
It requires an audience to approve every major decision
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts a job's titles and money with a career's open-ended play.

questions.q: What does Carse say about being forced to play a game?
a: No one can force you, so you can quit a game at any time
Audiences can pressure players into finishing what they start
Only children are free to leave a game once it begins
Rules make quitting impossible until a winner is declared
questions.why: Lesson 2 says feeling trapped is something we convince ourselves of.

questions.q: Which activity does the summary call the ultimate infinite game?
a: Storytelling, because anyone can take it up and change it
Politics, because it never produces a final winner
Sports, because records can always be broken later
Money, because wealth can keep growing without limit
questions.why: Lesson 3 says a story has a life of its own and cannot be stopped.

questions.q: Which examples does the summary give of people quitting a finite game?
a: Minimalists, nomadic freelancers and singles in communes
Retired athletes, former politicians and wealthy investors
Students, apprentices and new employees
Artists, musicians and full-time writers
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists them as people who stepped away from status-driven scripts.
